section_summary: This section consists chiefly of 1940 diplomatic, military-intelligence, and naval reports monitoring Japanese personnel, shipping, commerce, propaganda, and diplomatic strategy throughout Latin America. Most posts found little unusual activity, but several reports highlighted Japanese plans to counter U.S. influence, expand trade and intelligence networks, recruit aviators, cultivate military ties, and investigate petroleum resources near the Panama Canal. The section also documents German and Italian influence, alleged irregularities within the Japanese Legation in Panama, and strong public opposition to Japanese petroleum technicians in Esmeraldas, Ecuador. A 1942 covering letter forwarding a sealed Chinese communication appears at the beginning.

subfiles.title: Forwarding a sealed communication from the Chinese Minister in Mexico
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.to: Dr. T. V. Soong, Chinese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards a sealed reply received through the American Embassy in Mexico City from the Chinese Minister there.
subfiles.summary: The Department encloses a sealed communication addressed to T. V. Soong. It explains that the American Embassy in Mexico City received the communication from the Chinese Minister in reply to Soong's earlier letter.

subfiles.title: Movement of Japanese citizens through Guatemala City during December 1939
subfiles.from: U.S. Naval Attaché, Guatemala
subfiles.about: Reports the air travel and official or commercial affiliations of several Japanese nationals moving through Central America.
subfiles.summary: The report records the December 1939 movements of Junichi Miyata, Kurow Itoh, Yamamoto, Yashichi Otani, Kanji Uchida, and another Japanese national. It notes Itoh's import-export role, Yamamoto's connection with Japan's Ministry of Industries and Commerce, and earlier intelligence-file references for several travelers.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in the Monterrey Consular District
subfiles.from: Department of State filing office
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Monterrey despatch concerning Japanese fishing interests and trade in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The note says Japanese activity in the Monterrey district was not considered exceptional. Japanese interests centered on obtaining fishing rights on Mexico's west coast and expanding commerce through purchases of Mexican oil and sales of Japanese goods.

subfiles.title: Movement of Japanese citizens in Central America during March 1940
subfiles.doc_type: naval attaché report with duplicate copy
subfiles.from: F. H. Lamson-Scribner, U.S. Naval Attaché
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese diplomatic, commercial, and private travelers recorded in Central America during March 1940.
subfiles.summary: The report traces Kosaku Midzusawa, Yashichi Otani, Kiyoshi Suzuki, Saburo Takahashi, Yoshisuke Isoda, and Hirono Hata through Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, El Salvador, and the Canal Zone. It identifies diplomatic roles, discusses a prospective Nicaraguan barter treaty, and supplies personal details and earlier movement references. Pages 4 and 5 are substantially duplicate copies of the same report.

subfiles.title: Circular inquiry concerning unusual Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.to: All chiefs of mission in the American republics
subfiles.about: Requests immediate reports on suspicious Japanese activity and possible German attempts to encourage anti-Japanese resentment.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks each mission to report unusual Japanese activities or changes in Japanese shipping and commerce. It also seeks indications that Germans are exploiting local nationalist resentment against Japanese residents and authorizes consultation with consular officers.

subfiles.title: Reply from Caracas on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Caracas; signed Scott
subfiles.about: Reports no suspicious Japanese or German activity in Venezuela.
subfiles.summary: The mission observes no unusual Japanese activities or shipping changes, although Japanese commercial missions have attempted to broaden Venezuelan trade. It finds no German encouragement of anti-Japanese resentment and notes that the Japanese colony numbers only about twenty people.

subfiles.title: Reply from Ciudad Trujillo on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Ciudad Trujillo; signed Hinkle
subfiles.about: Reports no suspicious Japanese activity in the Dominican Republic.
subfiles.summary: The mission states that no suspicious Japanese activity has occurred recently and that occasional NYK vessel calls continue normally. No German anti-Japanese activity has been observed, in part because almost no Japanese live in the country.

subfiles.title: Reply from San José on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, San José; signed Hornibrook
subfiles.about: Reports no specified suspicious activity but comments on a Japanese special ambassador and German propaganda in Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: The mission reports no current activity of the kind described in the Department's circular. A Japanese special ambassador and party remain in San José but appear to be receiving a cool welcome, while German propaganda on other subjects remains a concern.

subfiles.title: Reply from San Salvador on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, San Salvador; signed Frazer
subfiles.about: Reports no unusual Japanese activity, shipping, commerce, or German agitation in El Salvador.
subfiles.summary: The mission finds nothing new in Japanese activity, shipping, or commerce. It reports only two unofficial Japanese residents and fewer than fifty adult German Nazis in El Salvador, with no German interest in Japanese affairs.

subfiles.title: Reply from Bogotá on Japanese shipping
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Bogotá; signed Keith
subfiles.about: Reports no suspicious activity except the planned resumption of an Osaka Shosen Kaisha service to Cartagena.
subfiles.summary: The embassy and consulates found no sign of the activities specified by the Department. Cartagena nevertheless reported that the Osaka Shosen Kaisha Line intended to resume service from Brazil with the arrival of the Brazil Maru on June 22.

subfiles.title: Reply from Asunción on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Asunción; signed Howard
subfiles.about: States that there were no unusual Japanese activities to report.
subfiles.summary: This brief reply answers the Department's circular inquiry. It reports simply that no unusual activities had been detected.

subfiles.title: Reply from Guatemala City on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Guatemala City; signed Des Portes
subfiles.about: Reports no suspicious Japanese activity beyond a previously reported matter and requests a response to an earlier telegram.
subfiles.summary: The legation reports no suspicious Japanese activity in Guatemala except the matter covered by its May 9 telegram. Because Guatemala had virtually no Japanese activity or colony, it considered German agitation against Japanese residents impracticable.

subfiles.title: Reply from Montevideo on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Montevideo; signed Wilson
subfiles.about: Reports no unusual Japanese activity in Uruguay.
subfiles.summary: The mission acknowledges receipt of the circular through Buenos Aires. It states that there were no unusual activities to report.

subfiles.title: Reply from Santiago on Japanese activity and military proposals
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Santiago; signed Bowers
subfiles.about: Reports little Japanese activity in Chile and the rejection of Japanese military-exchange proposals.
subfiles.summary: The embassy reports few Japanese residents, no anti-Japanese agitation, and no verifiable unusual ship movements. Chile had rejected a Japanese proposal to send a military training mission and an offer to host ten Chilean officers and their families in Japan at Japanese expense.

subfiles.title: Japanese diplomatic conferences in the Western Hemisphere
subfiles.from: J. M. Churchill, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.about: Reports planned Japanese diplomatic conferences intended to coordinate policy in the Americas and reduce dependence on the United States.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says Japan's Foreign Office, apparently at the initiative of its ambassador in Washington, called conferences of representatives in the Western Hemisphere. Their agenda included coordinating missions, modifying the American attitude toward Japan, and reducing Japanese economic dependence on the United States. It identifies a May conference in Rio de Janeiro and a later Washington conference involving chiefs of mission and Foreign Office representatives.

subfiles.title: Reply from Mexico City on Japanese and German activities
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Mexico City; signed Boal
subfiles.about: Reports no German agitation or unusual Japanese trade and shipping in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Mexican consular posts found no evidence that Germans were provoking conflict between Mexicans and Japanese. They likewise reported no unusual Japanese commercial or shipping developments, including in the Federal District.

subfiles.title: Reply from Port-au-Prince on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Port-au-Prince; signed Mayer
subfiles.about: Reports no Japanese shipping, commerce, or activities in Haiti.
subfiles.summary: The mission has nothing to report in response to the Department's circular. It states that Haiti had no Japanese shipping, commerce, or other activity.

subfiles.title: Japanese shipping agency reportedly reserved for German sympathizers
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Bogotá; signed Keith
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese Legation would award an Osaka Line agency only to Germans or known German sympathizers.
subfiles.summary: The consul at Cartagena reports that a Colombian firm's request for an Osaka Line agency received a written answer from the Japanese Legation. According to the report, the agency would be granted only to Germans or recognized German sympathizers.

subfiles.title: Japanese commerce and shipping in Nicaragua
subfiles.from: Meredith Nicholson, U.S. Legation, Managua
subfiles.about: Reports minimal Japanese activity in Nicaragua and intelligence that two Japanese Army aviation officers were recruiting pilots in the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Nicholson reports only one Japanese merchant in Nicaragua, occasional Japanese vessels at Corinto, and sporadic fishing-boat visits. The Chinese consul-general nevertheless advised that two Japanese Army aviation officers left Tokyo on March 22 to recruit pilots in Central and South America. Their location was unknown, and they had apparently not passed through Managua.

subfiles.title: Unusual and suspicious Japanese activities in Panama
subfiles.from: William Dawson, U.S. Embassy, Panama
subfiles.about: Reports a shipping-agency transfer, concern about German activity in the Canal Zone, and alleged financial irregularities at the Japanese Legation.
subfiles.summary: The NYK agency was transferred from Hapag Lloyd to the American firm Norton, Lilly and Company, leaving the German agency without shipping business but with its personnel intact. Dawson describes Hapag Lloyd as a center of German influence and recommends attention to its continued Canal Zone presence. He also reports rumors of a $20,000 shortage in Japanese Legation accounts, recalls of officials, and conflict between military and civilian factions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning Masao Matsumoto and Japanese Legation officials
subfiles.from: L. A. McIntire, Civil Intelligence Section, Panama Canal
subfiles.about: Describes alleged Japanese Legation embezzlement, recalls of officials, and an altercation aboard the Argentina Maru.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum claims Matsumoto investigated a $20,000 shortage that led to the recall of Yashichi Otani, Kiyoshi Suzuki, and Minister Kosaku Midzusawa. It alleges that Midzusawa encouraged intoxicated former fishermen to provoke Matsumoto aboard the Argentina Maru before a Canal Zone policeman ended the disturbance. Catalino Kiobiyama is characterized as a Japanese government official and aide, while Kanzo Nonaka is identified as a local barber-society president.

subfiles.title: Liquidation of German firms in Latin America
subfiles.from: Pierre de L. Boal, U.S. Embassy, Mexico
subfiles.about: Refers the Department to a commercial attaché's report indicating cordial German-Japanese relations.
subfiles.summary: Boal asks the Department to consult the commercial attaché's May 25 report on the liquidation of German firms in Latin America. He states that the report suggests relations between Germans and Japanese remained cordial.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Brazil
subfiles.from: Ware Adams for the U.S. Ambassador, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese diplomatic conferences, shipping, trade, cotton purchases, and propaganda in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: The embassy reports a recent conference of Japanese diplomatic and consular officers from Brazil, Argentina, Chile, and Peru. Shipping had increased moderately for the São Paulo cotton crop, while bilateral trade remained comparatively steady and increasingly important to Brazil's cotton exports. Japanese propaganda had expanded since the war began, and a clearing agreement may have been discussed.

subfiles.title: German and Japanese activities in Pará
subfiles.from: Randolph Harrison, Jr., for the U.S. Ambassador, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Transmits a vice-consular report on German and Japanese activities in Pará.
subfiles.summary: The embassy forwards a May 21 communication from the American vice consul at Pará. The enclosure addresses Japanese commercial activity and recent German and Nazi organizing in the district.

subfiles.title: Report from Pará on German and Japanese activities
subfiles.from: T. Muldrup Forsyth, American Vice Consul, Pará
subfiles.to: Jefferson Caffery, U.S. Ambassador, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports little Japanese activity but increased public visibility and organizing by Germans and Nazis in Pará.
subfiles.summary: Forsyth finds no unusual Japanese activity, shipping change, or significant effort to expand imports. Germans had become more conspicuous after military successes in Europe, and Nazis reportedly held meetings and tried to organize former Integralistas. No German effort to foster resentment against the mostly rural Japanese population was detected.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Chile
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Transmits consular reports from Concepción and Valparaíso on Japanese activity in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Bowers submits replies from Vice Consul McLain at Concepción and Consul McNiece at Valparaíso. The enclosures assess Japanese residents, firms, trade, shipping, and the prospects for anti-Japanese agitation.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Concepción
subfiles.from: Camden L. McLain, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Reports a small Japanese community and no suspicious activity in the Concepción district.
subfiles.summary: McLain identifies five known Japanese residents—a pair of merchants, a street vendor, a mechanic, and a farm manager—and finds no suspicious conduct. He discusses the firm Kandá, Watanabe y Cía., a dairy owned by Yoshitaro Amano, and the absence of Japanese shipping interests at Concepción or Talcahuano. Local newspapers had not promoted anti-Japanese sentiment.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities and shipping at Valparaíso
subfiles.from: Renwick S. McNiece, American Consul
subfiles.about: Reports normal Japanese activity at Valparaíso and evaluates shipping, cargo, and the likelihood of racial agitation.
subfiles.summary: McNiece finds no suspicious Japanese activity or major shipping changes, although the K.K.K. Line had reduced frequency and the NYK Line maintained monthly service. The Yasukuni Maru was expected in July, and a Japanese ship had unsuccessfully attempted to load tin ore. Because Chile had few Japanese residents and benefited economically from Japanese trade, he considered German-inspired racial agitation unlikely.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in the Mexicali Consular District
subfiles.from: Department of State filing office, citing Moore at Mexicali
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report describing the small, established Japanese farming population around Mexicali.
subfiles.summary: The underlying despatch characterized most Japanese residents as small farmers and long-term legal residents. It judged them unlikely to generate serious U.S.-Mexican friction, while warning that specially assigned agents might do so.

subfiles.title: German and Japanese activities in Bolivia
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, U.S. Legation, La Paz
subfiles.about: Reports little unusual Japanese activity but extensive concern about German military propaganda and foreign advisers in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: Jenkins reports no exceptional Japanese conduct or German campaign against Japanese residents, but describes Major Lehmann's propaganda among Bolivian Army officers and advocacy of fascist organization. Chilean, British, and Bolivian officials expressed concern about Lehmann's influence, while other German and Italian military personnel also presented potential risks. Japanese matters included a sample arms shipment, an influential La Paz community, and a Mitsui representative's view that the Lima disturbances arose from retail competition.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum for Japanese-activities report
subfiles.from: Liaison Officer, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests that an attached report be forwarded to the Office of Naval Intelligence after War Department review.
subfiles.summary: The State Department liaison officer sends an attachment to the War Department. The note asks that it subsequently be transmitted to the Navy Department's Office of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in São Paulo and Santos
subfiles.from: Carol H. Foster, American Consul General, São Paulo
subfiles.to: Jefferson Caffery, U.S. Ambassador, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports unusually active Japanese propaganda and travel but generally normal trade and shipping in São Paulo and Santos.
subfiles.summary: Foster reports intensified Japanese propaganda and an unusual number of Japanese travelers during the previous year. Japanese imports at Santos rose modestly, shipping schedules remained broadly stable, and only two extra cotton vessels were expected instead of the previous year's eight. No German effort to encourage anti-Japanese feeling had been observed.

subfiles.title: Department of State routing cover sheet
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics, Department of State
subfiles.to: Department officials including Duggan and Welles
subfiles.about: Routes a strictly confidential report concerning Japanese plans in the American republics.
subfiles.summary: The page is an internal State Department circulation sheet rather than a substantive report. It records handling by the American Republics and Far Eastern Affairs divisions and marks the material strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Japanese plans for penetration in the American republics
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.to: Chief of Staff and listed recipients
subfiles.about: Summarizes intelligence on Japanese plans formulated at the May 1940 Rio de Janeiro diplomatic conference.
subfiles.summary: Miles reports that Japanese diplomats in Rio reviewed the full range of Japanese activity in South America and planned future measures in light of relations with the United States. The projected program sought to restrain American influence, and an attached memorandum reproduced the objectives sent to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Program adopted at the Japanese diplomatic conference in Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.from: Japanese Ambassador in Rio de Janeiro, as reported by U.S. intelligence
subfiles.about: Sets out a broad Japanese political, economic, intelligence, cultural, and organizational program for Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The program calls for cultivating influential politicians, countering American propaganda, cooperating selectively with Italy, Spain, and Portugal, strengthening military contacts, selling arms, and inviting missions from Chile. Economic measures include credit institutions, expanded commercial staffs, regulated exporters, infrastructure projects, resource surveys, manufacturing plants, and Japanese control of shipping agencies. It also proposes a Domei news office, stronger broadcasts, intelligence exchanges about communism, cultural agreements and exchanges, new diplomatic posts, and recurring inter-American conferences.

subfiles.title: No suspicious Japanese activities in Honduras
subfiles.from: John D. Erwin, U.S. Legation, Tegucigalpa
subfiles.about: Reports no unusual Japanese activity or German agitation in Honduras while noting gradually increasing Japanese trade.
subfiles.summary: Erwin reports almost no Japanese residents, no suspicious conduct, and no exceptional activity at Puerto Cortés or La Ceiba. Japanese textiles and other imports had increased gradually, but without a sudden change. Germans were keeping a low profile, and President Carías's pro-Allied government was expected to suppress hostile propaganda quickly.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Argentina
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese shipping changes, cultural diplomacy, and the absence of notable anti-Japanese sentiment in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Armour finds little local resentment against Japanese residents, even after a dispute involving 108 Chinese seamen. Osaka Shosen Kaisha had altered its fleet and shortened the Buenos Aires–Los Angeles schedule, while the Yamashita Line remained unchanged. The Japanese government also offered exceptional travel and lodging facilities for five Argentine professors visiting Japan and Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Japanese vessels touching at Argentine ports
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Lists Osaka Shosen Kaisha and Yamashita Line vessels serving Argentine ports.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure names the Japanese vessels assigned to the Argentine trade. It identifies the Argentina Maru and Brazil Maru as new vessels and marks several ships as recently withdrawn.

subfiles.title: Compañía Minera Petrolera del Pacífico
subfiles.from: Boaz Long, U.S. Legation, Quito
subfiles.about: Transmits reports and commentary on Japanese geologists and an Ecuadorian petroleum-concession company operating in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: Long forwards an anonymous warning, confidential comments, and newspaper reports concerning Japanese technicians in Esmeraldas. He describes the Pacific Petroleum Mining Company as Ecuadorian but controlled by influential Colombian stockholders and possibly interested more in trading concessions than developing oil. American geologist Benjamin Franklin Wallis questioned the company's capital and contrasted it with Colonel Morris's development plans; Long requests instructions.

subfiles.title: Anonymous warning about Japanese soldiers in Ecuador
subfiles.from: “Ecuatorianos, amantes de la Paz y tranquilidad”
subfiles.about: Alleges that Japanese soldiers disguised as agricultural workers were entering Ecuador to threaten the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: The Spanish-language letter claims Japanese Army and Navy aviators were posing as farmers in Esmeraldas under an agreement involving the German Franz Spillmann. It alleges a plan to bring thousands of Japanese soldiers near the Panama Canal and accuses the Italian military mission of preparing a fascist coup and fifth column. The writers urge immediate American intervention.

subfiles.title: Confidential comments on Japanese technicians and the Ecuadorian government
subfiles.from: Confidential adviser or informant
subfiles.about: Evaluates the anonymous warning and urges investigation and expulsion of Japanese petroleum technicians in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: The writer rejects the claim that Ecuador's government was inherently fascist but acknowledges that Italian and some European advisers had spread fascist or Nazi ideas. He identifies Franz Spillmann and several Japanese as technicians for the Colombian-controlled Compañía Minera Petrolera del Pacífico, which held extensive concessions. He recommends interrogation, expulsion, restrictions on Japanese participation in Ecuadorian petroleum, and protection of the information source.

subfiles.title: El Día report on Japanese geologists in Esmeraldas
subfiles.from: El Día
subfiles.about: Reports official confirmation that Japanese technicians were employed for mineral exploration because American experts were too expensive.
subfiles.summary: The clipping states that Japanese geologists were working in Esmeraldas. Foreign Ministry sources explained that American technicians could not be hired at acceptable salaries and denied that the employment necessarily had international or political significance.

subfiles.title: El Telégrafo article on the Esmeraldas oil concession
subfiles.from: El Telégrafo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese technicians working on an Esmeraldas oil concession might represent a broader penetration effort near the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: The article says Ecuadorians Martínez and Delgado engaged Franz Spillmann and seven Japanese for work on a large concession, with more Japanese expected. It questions whether the named concessionaires were fronts and warns that economic activity might conceal strategic observation close to the Panama Canal. The paper calls for a government investigation and opposition to Asian immigration.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Esmeraldas
subfiles.from: Alfred T. Nester, American Consul, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Transmits Ecuadorian press reports on public reaction to Japanese activity in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: Nester refers to his earlier report to the Quito legation. He encloses copies and translations of reports from El Telégrafo and El Universo describing opposition to Japanese technicians in Esmeraldas.

subfiles.title: El Universo report on the Esmeraldas protest
subfiles.from: El Universo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Reports police dispersal of a protest against a Japanese petroleum mission in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: Residents protested the arrival of a Japanese mission studying petroleum deposits and described it as dangerous immigration comparable to developments in Peru. Police dispersed the crowd, but a public meeting was planned at the Municipal Theatre. The Japanese party departed under police protection while local inhabitants vowed further opposition.

subfiles.title: El Telégrafo report on suspected Japanese penetration
subfiles.from: El Telégrafo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Reports public alarm in Esmeraldas over alleged secret Japanese activity and plans for a protest meeting.
subfiles.summary: The report says residents suspected the Japanese of conducting secret maneuvers that might threaten Ecuador or another American country. The provincial police chief asked demonstrators to postpone action until the national government issued instructions, while a Municipal Theatre meeting remained planned. An excerpt from El Cosmopolita accused unnamed interests of being corrupted by Japanese money.

subfiles.title: El Universo clipping on alleged dangerous Japanese activity in Esmeraldas
subfiles.from: El Universo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Publishes allegations that Franz Spillmann and Japanese associates were seeking petroleum or gold under suspicious circumstances in Esmeraldas.
subfiles.summary: The Spanish clipping reports claims that Spillmann misrepresented archaeological or mineral work at Tolita and later returned with Japanese companions. It presents the activity as a sensitive matter of national interest requiring government action.

subfiles.title: El Telégrafo clipping on public opposition in Esmeraldas
subfiles.from: El Telégrafo, Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Prints the Spanish original of the report on protests against alleged Japanese penetration.
subfiles.summary: The clipping describes alarm over Japanese activity and fears of secret maneuvers connected with international conflict. It says the police chief sought postponement of a demonstration while citizens planned to deliberate at the Municipal Theatre.

subfiles.title: Secret report on Japanese recruitment of aviators
subfiles.from: Gordon B. McCoy, Lieutenant Colonel, U.S. Army
subfiles.about: Relays intelligence that Japanese officers were ordered to recruit aviators or military personnel in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source reported secret Japanese orders to two colonels to proceed to Latin America and recruit qualified citizens or residents for Japanese service. The analyst considered Japan's need for extra aviators unnecessary for operations against China and suggested preparations for another theater, possibly the Dutch East Indies. The memorandum recommends further inquiry in Latin America; several names and phrases are badly degraded in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Movements of Japanese nationals recorded by the Naval Attaché
subfiles.from: F. H. Lamson-Scribner, U.S. Naval Attaché, Guatemala
subfiles.about: Reports the movements and commercial roles of Shunichi Yamamoto, Yoshitaro Amano, and Y. Megurikami.
subfiles.summary: Yamamoto traveled from Managua through Guatemala City toward Brownsville while promoting Mitsui compensation trade. Amano returned through Limón and was identified as the owner of a fishing boat at Puntarenas. Megurikami, the Japanese import-export federation's representative in Costa Rica, was expected to transfer to Ecuador because of better commercial prospects.

subfiles.title: Japanese diplomatic approach to Latin American governments
subfiles.from: Pierre de L. Boal, U.S. Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese instructions urging Latin American governments to resist dependence on the United States and remain politically impartial.
subfiles.summary: The Chinese Minister supplied four Japanese arguments: diversify economic dependence, develop Far Eastern trade, avoid political or military agreements that might draw countries into the European war, and treat North America, Europe, and the Far East impartially. General Hay confirmed that the Japanese Minister had made a similar, friendly-toned approach. Hay contrasted it with a German note threatening consequences if Mexico were unfriendly at the Havana Conference.

subfiles.title: Transmitting a letter from the Chinese Minister in Havana
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Forwards Chinese intelligence about Japanese efforts to obstruct U.S. influence and the Havana Conference.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith transmits a July 16 letter from the Chinese Minister and notes that the Japanese chargé had recently sent identical coded messages to Japanese missions throughout the American republics. He suggests that the Chinese information might help the Office of Naval Intelligence decode those messages.

subfiles.title: Chinese warning about Japanese instructions for the Havana Conference
subfiles.from: Ti-Tsun Li, Chinese Minister in Cuba
subfiles.about: Warns that Japan instructed its Latin American diplomats to frustrate U.S. influence and undermine the Havana Conference.
subfiles.summary: Li reports that Foreign Minister Arita ordered Japanese representatives to resist extension of U.S. influence in Central and South America. The diplomats were to argue for diversified trade, greater commerce with the Far East, avoidance of U.S. political or military alliances, and impartiality among world regions. Li asks that the information reach the U.S. delegation and requests an interview with Secretary Cordell Hull.

subfiles.title: Japanese firms in Mexico
subfiles.from: Mexico City report by McGregor
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on Japanese firms and activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains no substantive narrative beyond its filing subject. It directs researchers to a June 28 Mexico City report concerning Japanese firms.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in Veracruz
subfiles.from: Veracruz despatch by Cochran
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on the end of a Japanese-backed petroleum venture and Japanese interest in strategic minerals.
subfiles.summary: The underlying despatch found almost no sign of Japanese activity in Veracruz. It noted the termination of the Compañía Petrolera Veracruzana, reportedly organized by Japanese interests, and an unconfirmed report that a Japanese traveler with a diplomatic passport investigated mica and antimony in southern Oaxaca.
